text: Welcome to Lecture 4 on Searching and Sorting. In an array of size n, linear search takes O(n) time because in the worst case we inspect every single element.

Binary search works by maintaining low and high bounds on a sorted array. At each iteration, we calculate mid = low + (high - low) / 2 and eliminate half of the remaining elements. Thus the runtime is strictly O(log n) compared to linear search which takes O(n).

Now let's examine Binary Search Trees. In a BST, every node in the left subtree has a value strictly less than the root, and every node in the right subtree is greater. In-order traversal visits nodes in sorted ascending order.

Graph traversals differ from tree traversals because graphs can contain cycles. Breadth-First Search (BFS) uses a FIFO queue to discover shortest paths in unweighted graphs, while Depth-First Search (DFS) uses a recursion call stack exploring as deep as possible along each branch.
